title: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container, and what is actually inside an image (layers, base image, app, dependencies)?
shortTitle: Docker Image Versus Container and What Is Inside an Image

s1_definition.profdef: A Docker image is an immutable, read-only template that packages everything needed to run an application: a base operating-system layer, runtime and dependencies, the application itself, and metadata such as the entrypoint and environment. A Docker container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image, with a thin writable layer on top where runtime changes live. The relationship is like a class and an object: the image is the definition built once, and a container is a live instance created from it; you can run many containers from the same image. An image is built from ordered, cached layers, each produced by a Dockerfile instruction, stacked via a union filesystem.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's standard new-branch blueprint. The image is the sealed, approved blueprint plus a kit containing everything a branch needs: the building shell (base OS), the furniture and machines (runtime and dependencies), the staff handbook (your application), and a note on how to open for business (entrypoint). A container is an actual branch built from that blueprint and now open and serving customers; the day's cash drawer and paperwork are the thin writable layer that is specific to that one running branch. You can open ten identical branches from the same blueprint, and when a branch closes, the blueprint is untouched and ready to open another.
s1_definition.oneliner: An image is the immutable layered template built once, and a container is a running instance of that image with a thin writable layer on top.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Docker image is an immutable, read-only template that packages everything needed to run an application: a base operating-system layer, runtime and dependencies, the application itself, and metadata such as the entrypoint and environment. A Docker container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image, with a thin writable layer on top where runtime changes live. The relationship is like a class and an object: the image is the definition built once, and a container is a live instance created from it; you can run many containers from the same image. An image is built from ordered, cached layers, each produced by a Dockerfile instruction, stacked via a union filesystem.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's standard new-branch blueprint. The image is the sealed, approved blueprint plus a kit containing everything a branch needs: the building shell (base OS), the furniture and machines (runtime and dependencies), the staff handbook (your application), and a note on how to open for business (entrypoint). A container is an actual branch built from that blueprint and now open and serving customers; the day's cash drawer and paperwork are the thin writable layer that is specific to that one running branch. You can open ten identical branches from the same blueprint, and when a branch closes, the blueprint is untouched and ready to open another.

**One line to remember:** An image is the immutable layered template built once, and a container is a running instance of that image with a thin writable layer on top.

sections.s2_technical:
An image is immutable and read-only. Once built, its contents never change; if you need a change you rebuild and get a new image with a new ID. This immutability is what makes deployments reproducible: the exact image tested in QA is byte-for-byte the one that runs in Prod. Images are identified by a content digest (a SHA256) and usually also by human-friendly tags like `transfer-service:1.2.0`.

A container is a runtime instance of an image. When you run an image, the engine creates a container by stacking a thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers and starting the process defined by the entrypoint. Anything the process writes, such as temp files or logs, goes into that writable layer, which is discarded when the container is removed unless you mount a volume. Because the writable layer is thin and the read-only layers are shared, you can run many containers from one image cheaply, and they are isolated from each other by the kernel.

Inside an image are ordered layers. Each layer is a filesystem diff produced by one image-building instruction. A typical banking-service image has: a base image layer such as `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` providing a minimal Linux plus the Java runtime; one or more layers adding dependencies; a layer copying the application artifact such as the JAR; and metadata layers that set the working directory, environment, exposed port, and entrypoint. The layers are stacked with a union filesystem so the running container sees them merged into one coherent filesystem.

Layer caching is a key property. Because each layer is content-addressed and cached, rebuilding only re-executes layers whose inputs changed and reuses the rest. This is why Dockerfile ordering matters: you copy and resolve dependencies before copying fast-changing source, so a code change does not invalidate the expensive dependency layer. Layers are also shared across images, so if two banking services share the same base image, that base is stored and pulled once.

The image also carries metadata, not just files. The image configuration records the default command or entrypoint (for example `java -jar /app.jar`), environment variables, exposed ports, the working directory, and labels. This is why running an image needs no extra instructions: everything required to start the process is baked into the image config.

A senior nuance is that secrets and build-time junk must not end up in layers, because every layer is readable by anyone who can pull the image and persists even if a later layer deletes the file. This is why multi-stage builds and careful layering matter: you keep build tools in a discarded stage and copy only the final artifact into the runtime image. Another nuance is that the writable layer should stay small and ephemeral; persistent state belongs in mounted volumes or external stores, never in the container's writable layer, so a container remains disposable. A third nuance is image provenance: in banking you pin base images by digest, scan them, and sign them, so you can prove exactly what is inside a production image.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India team used to deploy by copying a JAR onto a server where the Java version and OS libraries differed between environments, so the transfer service behaved differently in QA and Prod. This is exactly the problem an image solves. The image bundles the exact runtime, dependencies, and app into one immutable template, so every environment runs the identical thing.

Problem 2 — Engineers were confused about why "the image" was not changing when they restarted a container, or why data written in one container vanished. This is exactly the image-versus-container distinction. The image is the fixed template; the container is a disposable instance whose writable layer is lost on removal, which is why state must go to a volume or external store.

Problem 3 — Rebuilds were slow because a one-line code change re-downloaded all dependencies. This is exactly the problem layer caching and ordering solve. Copying and resolving dependencies in an earlier layer than the source means a code change only rebuilds the cheap top layers.

To make this concrete we will write a Java simulation that models the image and container concepts. We will model an `ImageLayer`, an immutable `Image` built from ordered layers with metadata (entrypoint), and a `Container` that is an instance of an image with its own thin writable layer. We will build one transfer-service image, run two containers from it, write different runtime data into each writable layer to show isolation, and show that removing a container discards its writable layer while the image is untouched and can spawn another container. This mirrors the real class-versus-instance relationship.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.docker.DockerConceptDemo

# Real Docker usage:
docker build -t transfer-service:1.2.0 .         # build the image once
docker history transfer-service:1.2.0            # inspect its layers
docker run -d --name c1 transfer-service:1.2.0   # run container 1
docker run -d --name c2 transfer-service:1.2.0   # run container 2 (same image)
docker rm -f c1                                  # remove c1; image untouched
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a Dockerfile-equivalent set of ordered layers, built into one image, then run as multiple containers.

Step 1: The image is constructed from four ordered layers: the base JRE, the dependency libs, the application JAR, and a metadata layer setting the port, plus an entrypoint of `java -jar /app.jar`. The layer list is copied defensively so the image is immutable. At this point we have one read-only template.

Step 2: The layers are printed in order, showing base, then dependencies, then application, then metadata. These layers are read-only and will be shared by every container run from this image.

Step 3: Two containers, c1 and c2, are created from the same image and started. Each prints that it started from `transfer-service:1.2.0` with the baked-in entrypoint, needing no extra instructions because the start command lives in the image metadata.

Step 4: Each container writes a temp file into its own writable layer. c1 writes a c1-specific log and c2 writes a c2-specific log. Printing each writable layer shows they contain only their own data, proving the writable layers are isolated per container even though the read-only layers are shared.

Step 5: Container c1 is removed. Its writable layer, with its one item, is discarded, demonstrating that runtime state in the writable layer is ephemeral. The log notes the image is unchanged.

Step 6: A third container, c3, is created and started from the same image, proving the image is still intact and can spawn new instances after one was removed. This is the class-versus-instance relationship in action.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Dockerfile (ordered instructions)
    │ docker build
    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ IMAGE transfer-service:1.2.0  │  immutable, read-only
  │  L1 base: temurin:21-jre      │
  │  L2 deps: /app/libs           │  ◀ shared across all containers
  │  L3 app:  /app.jar            │
  │  L4 meta: ENV + ENTRYPOINT    │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
       docker run │ (one image → many instances)
     ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
     ▼            ▼             ▼
  Container c1  Container c2  Container c3
  +writable L   +writable L   +writable L   ◀ thin, isolated, ephemeral
  (c1 logs)     (c2 logs)     (c3 logs)
     │ rm c1
     ▼
  c1 writable layer DISCARDED; image + other containers untouched
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Image/Container Classes ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Prototype/Factory: Image.run() produces Container instances     │
  │  Immutable Object: Image copies its layers, never mutates        │
  │  Class vs Instance: Image = definition, Container = live object  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: ImageLayer = one layer, Image = template, Container = run    │
  │  O: new layer type? add ImageLayer, no Container change          │
  │  D: Container depends on Image abstraction for its read-only base│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │        Image             │ run()  │       Container          │
  │ - tag: String            │───────▶│ - name: String           │
  │ - layers: List<ImageLayer>│       │ - image: Image           │ ◇ shares layers
  │ - entrypoint: String     │        │ - writableLayer: List    │ ◆ owns writable
  │ + run(name): Container   │        │ + start() / write()      │
  └───────────┬──────────────┘        │ + remove()               │
              │ composed of           └──────────────────────────┘
              ▼ 1..*
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │        ImageLayer        │  - instruction, content (read-only)
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Container Lifecycle ────────────────────

  [CREATED] → start() → [RUNNING] → write() → [RUNNING w/ data]
      │                                           │ remove()
      │                                           ▼
      └──────────────────────────────────→ [REMOVED] (writable layer gone)
  (Image stays IMMUTABLE throughout)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. new Image("transfer-service:1.2.0", layers, entrypoint)
  2. image.run("transfer-c1") → new Container(...)
  3. c1.start(); c1.write("...")       (writable layer only)
  4. image.run("transfer-c2") → isolated writable layer
  5. c1.remove() → writable layer discarded; image intact
  6. image.run("transfer-c3") → new instance still possible
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Docker image and a Docker container have the same relationship as a class and an object. The image is an immutable, read-only template built once that packages everything needed to run the application: a base operating-system layer, the runtime and dependencies, the application artifact itself, and metadata such as the entrypoint, environment, and exposed ports. A container is a running instance of that image; the engine stacks a thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers and starts the process defined by the entrypoint. You can run many containers from one image, and they are isolated from each other, which is exactly like creating many objects from one class.

What is actually inside the image is a stack of ordered layers, each being the filesystem change made by one Dockerfile instruction. A typical banking-service image has a base layer like a minimal Linux with the Java runtime, a layer or two adding dependencies, a layer copying the application JAR, and metadata recording how to start it. These layers are content-addressed and cached, which is why rebuild speed depends on ordering: you resolve dependencies in an earlier layer than you copy source, so a code change only rebuilds the cheap top layers and reuses the expensive dependency layer. Layers are also shared across images, so a common base is stored and pulled once.

The immutability is the practical payoff. Because the image never changes after it is built and is identified by a content digest, the exact image tested in QA is byte-for-byte the one that runs in Prod, which eliminated the old problem we had of a service behaving differently between environments because the server's Java version or OS libraries differed.

On the banking project this distinction mattered day to day. The transfer service was one immutable image promoted unchanged across dev, QA, and Prod, and we ran many containers from it behind a load balancer. The senior points I always add are that secrets and build tools must never end up in a layer, because every layer is readable by anyone who can pull the image and persists even if a later instruction deletes the file, which is why we use multi-stage builds and inject secrets at runtime; that persistent state belongs in mounted volumes or external stores, never in the container's ephemeral writable layer, so a container stays disposable; and that for provenance in banking we pin base images by digest, scan them, and sign them so we can prove exactly what is inside a production image.

---

keyPoints: Dockerfile: instructions to build an image
Multi-stage build: build in one stage, run in another — smaller image
Layer caching: order instructions for cache efficiency
COPY vs ADD: COPY is simpler and preferred
